blocks.text: FP16, 16-bit floating point, is a reduced precision numeric format that halves the memory of standard FP32 while roughly doubling computation speed on hardware that supports it, at the cost of a much narrower representable numeric range that requires careful handling during training.
This topic covers FP16 specifically, including the loss scaling technique needed to train stably with it, setting up a direct comparison with BF16, covered in the next topic of this module.
1. What FP16 Actually Represents
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472101915-981165108.png

FP16 stores each number using half the bits of standard 32-bit floating point, FP32, immediately halving the memory needed to store weights, activations, and gradients, directly connecting to the quantization ideas covered earlier in the LoRA and QLoRA module, though FP16 is used differently, typically for the active computation itself rather than just storage.
2. The Memory and Speed Benefits of FP16

blocks.alt: The Memory and Speed Benefits of FP16
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472101915-650783016.png

Beyond the direct memory savings, many modern GPUs include specialized hardware that processes FP16 computation notably faster than FP32, making FP16 training both more memory efficient and faster on hardware that supports this acceleration.
3. FP16's Limited Numeric Range
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472101915-655556080.png

The tradeoff for FP16 smaller size is a much narrower range of representable numbers compared to FP32, values that are either very large or very close to zero can fall outside what FP16 can accurately represent, a genuine risk during training where gradient values can span a wide range.

blocks.text: 4. Overflow and Underflow in FP16
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472101915-138461248.png

Overflow occurs when a value grows too large for FP16 to represent, while underflow occurs when a value shrinks so close to zero it gets rounded down to exactly zero, losing information entirely, both real risks during training since gradients, covered in the Causal Language Modeling Loss topic, can naturally vary widely in magnitude.
5. Loss Scaling, FP16's Companion Technique
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472102102-202292885.png

Loss scaling addresses underflow specifically, multiplying the loss by a large factor before backpropagation so the resulting gradients grow large enough to stay within FP16 representable range, then dividing the gradients back down by that same factor before actually applying the weight update.

code.content:
# A simplified loss scaling pattern for FP16 training
scale_factor = 1024
scaled_loss = loss * scale_factor
scaled_loss.backward()
for param in model.parameters():
    param.grad = param.grad / scale_factor
optimizer.step()

blocks.text: 6. FP16 in Mixed Precision Training
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472102103-895526881.png

Rather than running training entirely in FP16, mixed precision training keeps a master copy of the weights in full FP32 precision for the actual weight updates, while using FP16 for the faster forward and backward pass computation, combining FP16 speed benefits with FP32 stability where it matters most.

blocks.title: This connects directly to the earlier Mixed Precision Training topic
blocks.content: FP16 is one half of the mixed precision picture, the format used for fast computation, while the FP32 master weights provide the numeric stability needed for reliable weight updates over the course of training.

blocks.text: 7. Where FP16 Training Can Go Wrong

Without loss scaling, FP16 training can silently produce gradients that underflow to zero, effectively halting learning for those specific weights without any obvious error message, exactly the kind of subtle bug worth checking for if a model unexpectedly stops improving during an FP16 training run.
8. FP16 vs Full Precision, The Tradeoff

FP16 trades numeric range and simplicity for meaningful memory and speed gains, a worthwhile tradeoff for most fine-tuning workloads given loss scaling and mixed precision training address its main risks, though it does add implementation complexity compared to simply training in full FP32 throughout.
9. FP16's Place Relative to BF16
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472102103-826836231.png

BF16, covered directly in the next topic of this module, offers an alternative 16-bit format that avoids FP16 narrow range problem entirely, at the cost of some numeric precision, and understanding FP16 clearly here sets up a direct, meaningful comparison between the two formats.
Worked Example

A team training with FP16 notices their loss stops decreasing partway through training, with no clear error message. Investigating, they discover several gradient values had underflowed to exactly zero, effectively freezing those weights, because they had not enabled loss scaling.

After adding loss scaling to their training setup, retraining proceeds normally, with gradients staying within FP16 representable range throughout, confirming the earlier stall was specifically an underflow problem that loss scaling was designed to solve.
Common Mistakes

items: Training in FP16 without loss scaling and being confused by silent gradient underflow
Assuming FP16 always provides pure speed benefit without accounting for its narrower numeric range risk
Not keeping an FP32 master copy of weights, relying entirely on FP16 for weight updates and losing numeric stability
Confusing FP16 with the quantization techniques covered in the LoRA and QLoRA module, which serve a different, storage focused purpose

blocks.text: Practice
In your own words, explain why a gradient that is mathematically very small but nonzero could underflow to exactly zero once represented in FP16, and how loss scaling prevents that from happening.
Key Takeaway

FP16 halves memory usage and can meaningfully speed up computation on supporting hardware, but its narrow numeric range risks overflow and underflow during training, problems addressed through loss scaling and by keeping an FP32 master copy of weights for stable updates, together forming the mixed precision training approach many fine-tuning workflows rely on.
